notes.b: A few generations ago, marriage was expected of everyone and was the only accepted basis for living together and raising a family. Pressure from society, family and the Church has fallen, so people now treat marriage as a choice.
points: Couples now tend to marry later, often after completing their education and establishing a career. Some do not marry at all, because social, family and Church pressure to marry young has fallen.
Cohabitation, living together without being married, has become common and is widely accepted, because marriage is no longer seen as the only acceptable basis for a couple's life together.
Marriage is no longer seen as the only acceptable basis for a family, so many children are born to parents who are not married.
Legislation recognises cohabiting couples through the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010. Cohabitation still gives fewer legal rights than marriage.
Children born outside marriage are no longer treated differently in law, under the Status of Children Act 1987. In this way the law reflected, and helped to change, attitudes.
The 2015 marriage referendum allowed same-sex couples to marry, under the Marriage Act 2015, reflecting wider acceptance of different types of family.
notes.tip: Discussing the impact of changing attitudes to marriage on family life is asked at every level. Cover later marriage, cohabitation, divorce and separation, lone-parent and blended families, same-sex marriage, smaller families and more choice. Short questions may ask you to define cohabitation or give two reasons attitudes to marriage changed.

notes.b: Divorce only became possible in Ireland after the 1995 referendum. Attitudes changed, and the law followed, so married couples now have two legal routes when a marriage breaks down.
points: Divorce became legal in Ireland after a referendum in 1995 (carried narrowly, after an earlier referendum in 1986 had rejected divorce). The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 sets out the conditions for granting one.

Under that Act, a divorce may be granted only where three conditions are met. First, the spouses have lived apart for two of the previous three years, a period set by the Family Law Act 2019, in operation from 1 December 2019.
Second, there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, meaning the couple are unlikely to get back together.
Third, proper provision has been or will be made for the spouses and dependent children, so that nobody is left without support.
Judicial separation, provided for under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, as amended, allows spouses to live apart under a court order that deals with maintenance and property.
Judicial separation does not end the marriage, so neither spouse can remarry. Divorce does end the marriage.
notes.tip: To set out the conditions for a divorce, give three: living apart for the required period (now two of the previous three years), no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision for spouses and dependants. Remember that judicial separation does not end a marriage and divorce does.

notes.h: Effects of changing attitudes to marriage on family life
notes.b: Changed attitudes to marriage, cohabitation, separation and divorce have changed what families look like and how they feel to live in.
points: There are more lone-parent, blended (reconstituted, where partners bring children from earlier relationships) and cohabiting families, so family structures show more variety.
Families are smaller and first births come later, because couples marry later and plan when to have children.
There is more family breakdown, but also greater freedom to leave an unhappy or abusive marriage.
Children may live in more than one household when parents separate.
Family relationships are now chosen rather than expected, because people are less bound by duty to follow one set pattern.
There is less stigma (social disapproval) for lone parents than there once was.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions on the decline of the traditional family want reasons: separation and divorce, births outside marriage, fewer marriages, changing roles, contraception and urbanisation. Present change neutrally; do not say the older pattern was better or worse.

notes.b: Parenting has moved from strict authority towards partnership with children, and from mothers alone towards both parents and wider carers.
points: Parenting has become more child-centred, with greater emphasis on children's views, rights and wellbeing, open communication and negotiated rules instead of strict obedience.
Children's rights are recognised in the Constitution, through the Thirty-first Amendment (Children) 2012, which inserted Article 42A and was signed into law in 2015.
Physical punishment of children by parents is prohibited by Irish law: the Children First Act 2015 removed the defence of reasonable chastisement, so smacking is no longer lawful discipline.
Attitudes moved towards explaining, praising and setting limits. Child protection is the State's concern, carried out by Tusla, the Child and Family Agency.

Smaller families are now more common, as contraception and family planning let couples choose the number and timing of their children. The cost of rearing children and women's work also play a part, and each child gets more attention and money.

Mothers and fathers increasingly share childcare, and fathers are more involved in caring and housework. Paternity leave (the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016, two weeks) recognises the father's role.

Parental leave (the Parental Leave Act 1998) allows parents to take unpaid time off work to care for children. Paid Parent's Leave and Benefit (the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019) recognises both parents' role, and some men are the main carers (house husbands).

Grandparents often take on regular childcare, particularly where both parents work outside the home. Paid childcare (childminders, creches and after-school services) and pre-school education are also widely used.
notes.tip: Discussing changing attitudes to parenting is a common question. Cover the child-centred approach, shared parenting, fathers' leave, smaller families, and grandparents and childcare. On smacking, say the 2015 Act removed the defence of reasonable chastisement; do not say it created a new offence.

notes.h: Effects of changing parenting on family life
notes.b: A more open and shared style of parenting brings benefits, but it also puts new pressures on parents and changes the way children fit into the family.
points: Relationships are closer and more open, and decisions are more equal, because children's views are heard.
Children have greater independence, because they are given more say and more responsibility.
Working parents feel more pressure and guilt, a state sometimes called time poverty (never having enough time for everything).
Childcare costs money, which adds to the strain on family budgets.
There is less respect for traditional authority, because rules are negotiated rather than simply obeyed.
Children may take on more responsibility for chores, or for the care of younger siblings.

notes.b: Who earned, who cared and who decided used to be settled by gender. Attitudes have shifted towards sharing these jobs, which is the biggest change in everyday family life.
points: Traditional roles assigned the male as breadwinner (earner) and head of the household, and the female as homemaker and carer, with responsibilities kept largely separate. Children obeyed and helped, and older children minded younger ones.

Egalitarian roles (equal, shared roles) are now more common. Partners share earning, finances, housework, childcare, discipline and decisions, and both partners often work, which is the dual-earner family.
Men take a greater part in housework and childcare, while women take a greater part in paid work and decision-making.
A man taking on the role of house husband or primary carer, and a woman as main earner, are now socially accepted.
The decline in the influence of the Church lessened expectations about marriage, sexuality and parental roles.
Household tasks are shared with children, and older children may look after younger siblings.
Family diversity means that nuclear, extended, lone-parent, blended, cohabiting and same-sex-parent families are all recognised as families.
notes.tip: Describe the move from breadwinner and homemaker to equal partners, and include the effects of women working, house husbands and children's roles. Present traditional roles as different from today's, and say what changed; do not judge them as better or worse.

notes.h: Effects of changing roles on family life
notes.b: Shared roles bring clear gains, but they also create new tensions that families have to manage.
points: Relationships between partners are more equal, because tasks and decisions are shared.
Families have more income when both partners work.
Women gain greater independence, because earning their own money reduces reliance on a partner.
Role overload and role conflict (the strain of balancing work and home duties), time pressure and stress can follow when both partners work and also care for the family.
There can be arguments about sharing tasks, because the old rules about who does what no longer apply.
Some men feel a loss of status, because the breadwinner role is no longer theirs alone.

notes.b: Attitudes did not change by accident. Several developments in education, law, work and communication made new choices possible and acceptable.
points: Improved education, particularly for women, has widened choices about careers, marriage and having children.
Contraception and family planning allowed couples to control family size and plan or delay childbearing.
Women's participation in paid work, and equality legislation, gave women financial independence.
The decline in the influence of the Church and of tradition (secularisation) means that marriage, sexuality, cohabitation and divorce are now seen as personal choices.
Urbanisation (growth of towns and cities) and greater mobility loosened the influence of the extended family and the local community.
Media, travel and international influences, and communications technology, introduced new ideas about relationships and family life.
Greater personal freedom and individual choice came to be valued over duty to family or community. Higher living and housing costs now often require two incomes.
Legislation and referendums both reflect and speed up change: a law can follow a shift in attitudes and then help to make the new attitude normal.
notes.tip: Give two reasons attitudes to marriage changed when asked for a short answer, and remember that attitudes are different from laws: say that a law reflected or helped to change an attitude.

notes.h: Modern communications technology and family life
notes.b: Mobile phones, social media and video calls have changed how family members stay in touch and how they spend time together, with gains and losses.
points: Mobile phones, social media and video calls keep the extended family and emigrants in contact, so distance matters less to family relationships.
These technologies also allow remote working, which can give parents more flexibility.
Screen time can reduce face-to-face time, because family members may spend time together while each looks at a device.
Parents may find it harder to supervise children, because much online activity is private.
Cyberbullying and online safety are concerns for families.
notes.tip: For the impact of modern communications technology on family life, set contact and convenience against screen time and safety.

notes.h: Comparing family life a hundred years ago and today
notes.b: A direct comparison of the past and the present is a good way to see how attitudes have changed.
points: Compare roles, the number of children and attitudes to marriage a hundred years ago and today.
Interview an older relative about who earned, who cared and who made decisions in their childhood home.

keyTerms.definition: Living together as a couple without being legally married.
A pattern of family roles in which partners share responsibilities such as finances, housework and childcare equally.
A division of responsibilities in which the father earns the income and the mother runs the home and cares for children.
A court order allowing spouses to live apart, dealing with maintenance and property, without ending the marriage.
A family in which one parent lives with and cares for one or more children.
A family formed when a parent with children marries or cohabits with a partner who may also have children.
An approach to raising children that gives weight to their views, needs and participation in decisions.
A family made up of two parents and their children living together.
Methods used to prevent pregnancy, allowing couples to plan the number and timing of children.

factCards.term: Three conditions for granting a divorce under Irish law
factCards.definition: The spouses have lived apart for four of the previous five years, there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision has been made for the spouse and dependants.

factCards.term: Three shifts in attitudes to parenting
factCards.definition: More child-centred decision-making, shared childcare between mothers and fathers, and smaller family size.

factCards.term: Four causes of changing attitudes to family life
factCards.definition: Better education for women, contraception, urbanisation and mobility, and personal freedom.

factCards.term: Four types of modern family structure
factCards.definition: Nuclear, extended, lone-parent and blended families.

questions.prompt: Name two changes in attitudes to marriage in Ireland in recent decades.
questions.model: Couples marry later, often after completing education and establishing a career. Cohabitation without marriage is widely accepted. Many children are born to parents who are not married. Divorce is available under the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996.

questions.prompt: Explain how attitudes to parenting and to traditional family roles have changed, and describe the effects of these changes on children.
questions.model: Parenting has become more child-centred, with children's views and negotiated rules given weight, and physical punishment is prohibited by law. Smaller families, made possible by contraception, mean parents can give each child more attention. Traditional roles of male breadwinner and female homemaker have given way to egalitarian sharing of finances, housework, discipline and childcare, and fathers can take paternity leave. Children may gain more say in family decisions and may take on more household responsibility, or look after younger siblings. Where both parents work, children may rely more on grandparents or childcare services, and may experience less time with their parents.
